opus-5.5.text:
I think about it in layers. The most immediate layer is people who already work with 3D every day: game developers, indie studios, animators, people making assets for film and VFX, and increasingly folks doing AR/VR. For them, making a single good 3D model can take hours or even days. If we can turn that into minutes, that's a very direct and very valuable improvement to an existing workflow.

But honestly, I don't think the most exciting part of the opportunity is the existing 3D market. The existing market is limited by how hard 3D is. Very few people in the world can open Blender or Maya and produce something good. It's a steep learning curve. I spent years building Taichi, a graphics programming language, and even in that community you feel how high the barrier to entry is.

So the bigger layer is everyone who *wants* 3D content but has never been able to make it: e-commerce sellers who want 3D product views, educators, people with 3D printers at home, small businesses, hobbyists, kids who want to make their own game characters. When creation becomes as easy as typing a sentence or uploading a picture, the market isn't the number of 3D artists anymore. It's the number of people with an idea.

There's a good analogy with photography. Before smartphones, photography was a professional and enthusiast market. Once everyone had a camera in their pocket, the amount of visual content exploded by orders of magnitude, and entirely new industries were built on top of it. I think 3D is at a similar inflection point. Generative AI is the thing that lowers the cost of creation, and when cost drops dramatically, demand doesn't just grow linearly. New use cases appear that no one would have bothered with before.

Then there's the longer-term layer: if we really believe in spatial computing, in simulation, in embodied AI and robotics, then the world will need an enormous amount of 3D data and 3D environments. Today that content is basically handcrafted, which doesn't scale.

So my honest assessment is that the current market is meaningful but not huge. The market we're actually building toward is much larger, because we're helping to create it. As a startup, our job is to serve the professionals really well today, earn their trust, and make the product good enough that the much bigger wave of new creators can come in.

r001.rationale: The response discusses existing and potential user groups, but does not say that conversations with users reveal new ways to solve problems.

r002.rationale: The response describes a much larger future market driven by easier 3D creation and new use cases, but does not attribute an unlimited opportunity to Mesh’s adaptability.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I try not to start from a top-down TAM number, because those numbers tend to be either meaningless or flattering. The way I think about it is bottom-up, from the workflow we're actually replacing.

Mesh is about getting from an idea to a usable 3D asset without the bottleneck of a human spending hours or days in a modeling tool. So the first question is: how many people today are producing 3D content, and how much of their time goes into that grind? Games, film and animation, product visualization, architecture, e-commerce, industrial simulation. Each of those alone is a multi-billion dollar content pipeline, and 3D is the most expensive kind of asset in all of them. If you just took the existing spend on 3D asset creation and asked what fraction of it could be compressed by an order of magnitude, you'd already be looking at something very large.

But I actually think that framing undersells it. The more interesting part is the demand that doesn't exist yet because 3D is too hard. Every indie game developer who gave up on their art, every small brand that would love a configurable 3D product viewer but can't afford a studio, every educator or hobbyist who has an idea but not the skill. When the cost of making something drops by a hundred times, the market doesn't shrink proportionally, it explodes, because entirely new categories of creators show up. We saw this with photography when phones got cameras, and with video when editing became something you could do on your phone.

And then there's a third layer that I'm personally most excited about, which is that 3D assets are also what you need to train embodied AI, robotics, and simulation. The world is 3D. If we want AI systems that understand and act in physical space, they need enormous amounts of 3D data, and almost none of it exists at scale today. That's a market that's basically being created right now.

So my honest assessment is that the near-term opportunity is a clear and large one in professional content pipelines. The medium-term one is a creator economy that doesn't exist yet. And the long-term one might be the biggest of all, where 3D generation becomes infrastructure for AI understanding the physical world. I don't know exactly how to put a number on the second and third pieces, and I'm a bit suspicious of anyone who claims they can. But I'm confident the direction is right, and that's what matters when you're building.

r001.rationale: The response discusses existing workflows and new creator demand, but does not say that conversations with users reveal new ways to solve problems.

r002.rationale: The response describes a large and expanding market opportunity, but does not attribute potentially unlimited opportunity to Mesh’s adaptability.

astra-6.text:
I think the opportunity is much bigger than making existing 3D workflows faster. That’s an important starting point, because creating high-quality 3D content takes a lot of time and expertise. But if we can make that process much easier, we can also bring in people who would never have used traditional 3D tools.

So I’d look at the market in two parts. One is existing demand—people making games, films, or product visualizations. The other is new demand that becomes possible when creating a 3D asset is inexpensive and accessible. That second part is harder to quantify, but I think it could be very significant.

Of course, generating something interesting isn’t enough. People need assets they can actually use. For me, the key is whether we can consistently help users get from an idea to a useful result. That’s what turns a broad market opportunity into a business.

r001.rationale: The response discusses making 3D creation accessible, but does not say that conversations with users reveal new ways to solve problems.

r002.rationale: The response describes potentially significant new demand, but does not attribute an unlimited market opportunity to Mesh’s adaptability.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the opportunity is much bigger than making existing 3D workflows more efficient. Today, creating a 3D asset takes specialized skills and a lot of time, so many people who could use 3D content simply don’t create it.

Games, film, product design, and e-commerce already need these assets. But if we make creation easy enough that anyone can turn an idea into a 3D model, we can also expand the market. A small developer can build a richer game, or someone without modeling experience can create something for 3D printing.

So I would look at both the existing demand for professional 3D content and the new demand that emerges when the cost and skill barriers come down. That second part is harder to quantify, but I think it’s a very large opportunity.

r001.rationale: The response discusses existing and emerging demand, but does not say that conversations with users reveal new ways to solve problems.

r002.rationale: It describes a large opportunity from lowering creation barriers, but does not attribute that opportunity to Mesh’s adaptability.
